A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PCFG subgrammar-learning research. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite the changed title and extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original transformer-training experiments, representation analyses, recursion tests, and arithmetic evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results on PCFG learning, subgrammar pretraining, representations, and recursive generalization.

M1.justification: The autoregressive modeling and subgrammar-pretraining procedures remain unchanged. v2's architecture appendix supplies previously missing specifications without establishing a change to the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same experimental grammar definitions and the same PCFG-learning, pretraining, recursive-prefix, and arithmetic tasks. The renamed Outer Subgrammar Example matches v1's Unified Subgrammar Example.

E2.justification: The reported comparisons retain training from scratch versus subgrammar pretraining, including the same comparisons in the representation tables and Figure 6. The new nanoGPT citation identifies implementation provenance, not an additional evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Section 6 changes the reported arithmetic-test models from ChatGPT-5 Instant/Thinking to GPT-5.1 Instant/Thinking. This revises the stated experimental configuration, but unchanged scores and Appendix D.1's retained ChatGPT-5 heading do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 Section 4.1 newly reports checking subgrammar divergences with varying prefixes and obtaining similar outcomes. Conversely, v1 Figure 1(b)'s analysis with 30%, 30%, and 40% subgrammar occurrence probabilities is no longer displayed. The other recursion, pretraining, and prefix analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report 30 random seeds for the CKA analysis and 30-seed pretraining distributions. Uncertainty displays and statistical reporting practices remain unchanged; Table 1's new color highlighting does not introduce a significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: The loss trajectories in v1 Figure 1(b) are removed, while v2 adds a qualitative report of similar decomposition results across prefixes. Table 1, v1 Table 2/v2 Table 3, and Figures 2–7 retain their results. Arithmetic scores remain 5/5 versus 2/5 despite the changed model attribution.

T1.justification: v2 adds informal Corollary 4.7, giving a sufficient condition for parallel learning: updates for one subgrammar must not harm others. This substantially extends the theoretical treatment of training dynamics. Earlier decomposition proofs largely remain, but Definition 4.2 changes P_A to P_G, introducing an inconsistency with the retained subgrammar-based proof.

C1.justification: v1 claims that loss decomposition implies parallel subgrammar learning; v2 makes this implication conditional on additional strong assumptions. The abstract and introduction also redefine the contribution as extending existing CFG-learning research through subgrammar structure, rather than broadly initiating that research direction.

C2.justification: v2 explains possible statistical context-insensitivity despite failures on rare deep prefixes and explicitly separates loss decomposition from guarantees about optimization. New limitations identify restricted synthetic, unambiguous grammar coverage and clarify that arithmetic anecdotes are not direct evidence about recursive-PCFG training difficulty. Existing optimization-versus-capacity conjectures are retained.

D1.justification: New Appendix A and Table 2 provide nanoGPT provenance, model configurations, a 256-token context window, tokenization, dropout, AdamW settings, batch size, weight decay, gradient clipping, and checkpointing information. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation; they do not establish changes to previously conducted experiments.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly builds on Cagnetta and Wyart (2024) and Allen-Zhu and Li (2023), positioning subgrammar dynamics as its distinction from prior PCFG-transformer research. This substantially revises novelty positioning. It also adds nanoGPT attribution and removes references including Cottier, Grattafiori, Suzgun, and Tiwari.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, theoretical exposition, and closing discussion are extensively rewritten. Section 4 is reorganized, a Limitations section is added, and the appendices are reordered around new architecture documentation, existing proofs, grammar definitions, and experimental results.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout, substantially resizing and relocating displays. Figure 1 annotates the former panel (a) and removes panel (b); a configuration table is added, Table 1 gains colored highlights, and Figures 5–7 are consolidated on the final page.

improvement.justification: The new architecture appendix and clearer assumptions and limitations improve reproducibility and claim calibration. These gains are partly offset by the new P_A/P_G inconsistency in Definition 4.2, conflicting arithmetic-model attribution between Section 6 and Appendix D.1, and removal of Figure 1(b). The net improvement is therefore limited.
